No backpressure: queue.Queue() is unbounded and submit() never blocks, allowing unbounded memory growth/OOM if consumers ingest faster than workers process

Final offsets never committed on graceful shutdown: close() sets shutdown_event before draining, so the commit loop exits without a final commit pass, causing full redelivery of drained work on restart
No health-check or stall detection for the pipeline: no detection for persistent commit_function failures (offsets accumulate forever), poison groups backing up, and no alerting hooks
submit()'s error path can complete an offset it never added: if put() raises ShutDown after add_offset, the handler marks the dropped item complete, causing silent loss during shutdown
Integration tests mock the processor entirely, verifying plumbing but not the feature — no test verifies thread-queue-parallel produces the same application-level results as serial mode

Error-handling test asserts no commit for failed partition, contradicting implementation which calls complete_offset even on exception, so failed messages are silently skipped; no reliable test pins down intended at-least-once vs skip-on-error semantics

join() calls close() and shuts down the queue pool, deviating from arroyo strategy lifecycle where join should only wait for in-flight work; no test covers close/join/terminate lifecycle ordering

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy docstring claims 'Only commits offsets after successful processing' but the code commits offsets even on failure, violating the documented guarantee

The 'natural backpressure' claim is false because queues are unbounded (queue.Queue() has no maxsize), so submit never blocks and memory grows unboundedly if processing is slower than consumption

wait_until_empty / get_stats()['total_items'] == 0 is not a completion signal since qsize() == 0 only means items were dequeued and the worker may still be processing the last item, making tests that poll on this racy
wait_until_empty is dead code, never called anywhere
WorkItem.message is dead weight: set everywhere (forcing tests to construct fake Message objects) but never read, and it leaks arroyo KafkaPayload/Message types across the boundary

max_workers is semantically overloaded as 'number of queues' (hash shards) rather than thread count, so changing one meaning silently changes the other, and 'or 20' fallback means --max-workers 0 silently becomes 20
Dead/nonsensical except queue.ShutDown around the result processor callback, which cannot raise queue.ShutDown — leftover copy-paste obscuring the actual exception path
Commit thread is started in __init__, making the object impossible to construct without side effects (tests must always call close/shutdown or leak threads)
join() delegates to close(), conflating arroyo's join (wait for completion) with close (stop), so graceful draining isn't implemented and in-flight items are dropped when close runs
Shared FixedQueuePool is destroyed when any strategy closes/rebalances, shutting down all worker threads and queues for other still-live strategies, silently dropping messages on routine rebalances
join() calls close(), causing the shared pool to be shut down twice on normal graceful shutdown
OrderedQueueWorker.run completes the offset in the finally block even when result_processor raised, causing failed messages to be committed as processed (permanent silent data loss)
SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit's catch-all marks decode/grouping_fn failures as complete, committing offsets for failed messages
Test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling passes only by timing luck with an or-escape-hatch assertion, masking the data-loss bug (silent-pass verification mechanism)
If FixedQueuePool.shutdown races with a put, queue.Queue.put raises ShutDown in submit(), and the catch-all marks that offset complete, losing the message
Queues are unbounded (queue.Queue() with no maxsize), providing no backpressure despite the design claim, risking OOM under load
terminate() never joins the commit thread and never commits final offsets, losing up to the last second of processed offsets and racing with pool teardown
OffsetTracker's mark_committed never prunes outstanding offsets, so stale state after partition revoke/reassign can permanently block commits for that partition, stalling the consumer
There is no rebalance hook to reset or hand off OffsetTracker state
submit() catch-all converts every decoder/grouping_fn bug into silent message loss with only a log line, degrading ordering guarantees silently
hash(group_key) is process-randomized (PYTHONHASHSEED), breaking cross-process consistency and the docstring's consistent-hashing claim; should use a stable hash like md5
Test test_different_groups_distributed asserts an exact probabilistic distribution (all 3 queues hit), which is flaky
wait_until_empty checks qsize()==0 which does not mean items are processed (in-flight items), making it misleading/unsafe if used for shutdown

adjudication_records.issue_text: FixedQueuePool creates queue.Queue with no maxsize, so queues grow unboundedly causing unbounded memory growth and eventual OOM, contradicting the docstring's backpressure claim

adjudication.rationale: In `FixedQueuePool.__init__`, each worker queue is created as `queue.Queue()` with no `maxsize` (default is unbounded). In `submit`, items are enqueued via `work_queue.put(work_item)` which will not block for backpressure in an unbounded queue, allowing the producer to enqueue indefinitely if workers fall behind. This makes unbounded memory growth/OOM possible and contradicts the strategy docstring claim of “Natural backpressure when queues fill up.”

adjudication_records.issue_text: OffsetTracker.all_offsets and outstanding sets grow unboundedly when a gap or slow group stalls offset pruning in mark_committed

adjudication.rationale: In `OffsetTracker`, every submitted message adds its offset into `all_offsets` (and initially `outstanding`) via `add_offset`, but offsets are only removed from `all_offsets` in `mark_committed` (it filters `o > offset`). If committing cannot advance—e.g., an earlier offset remains outstanding for a long time (slow/hung work item) or an offset is never observed (gap relative to later observed offsets)—then `get_committable_offsets` will not return higher offsets, `mark_committed` won’t prune, and `all_offsets` (and potentially `outstanding`) will continue accumulating later offsets indefinitely as new messages are consumed/processed. This is a diff-grounded scalability/memory-growth concern in the new queue consumer implementation, even if gaps are unlikely in normal Kafka consumption.

adjudication_records.issue_text: WorkItem retains the full Kafka Message payload in memory for the item's lifetime in the queue, needlessly keeping the entire byte string alive

adjudication.rationale: In `queue_consumer.py`, `WorkItem` includes `message: Message[KafkaPayload | FilteredPayload]`, and `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit` populates it with the full Kafka `Message` (which contains the payload bytes). The worker (`OrderedQueueWorker.run`) never uses `work_item.message`, only `work_item.result`, `partition`, and `offset`, so queued items unnecessarily retain the full message/payload in memory for the lifetime of the queue item. This is a diff-grounded memory/performance concern rather than a functional defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Head-of-line blocking: a single slow group blocks all offset commits for the partition, degrading commit/memory-cleanup throughput with no timeout or cap

adjudication.rationale: In `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy._commit_loop`, offsets are only committed when `OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets()` finds a contiguous processed range per `Partition`. Because `OffsetTracker` tracks all offsets in a partition (`all_offsets` / `outstanding`) and requires completion of the earliest outstanding offset before advancing `last_committed`, any single slow/blocked work item with a low offset will prevent committing later offsets in that same partition, even if they finished on other queues (`FixedQueuePool` processes groups on different worker threads). While this is consistent with Kafka’s per-partition commit semantics, the diff shows no timeout/cap or eviction for long-outstanding offsets, so `all_offsets`/`outstanding` can grow and delay cleanup until the head item finishes.

adjudication_records.issue_text: get_committable_offsets performs an O(offset-span) linear scan per partition every second, causing steady CPU tax when consumer is degraded

adjudication.rationale: In `OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets`, the code computes `min_offset`/`max_offset` and then iterates `for offset in range(start, max_offset + 1)` checking membership in `all_offsets`/`outstanding` sets. This is O(max_offset-start) per partition (i.e., proportional to the numeric offset span), not O(number of tracked offsets). The `_commit_loop` in `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` calls this every ~1s (`shutdown_event.wait(1.0)`), so if a partition accumulates a large sparse span (e.g., after degradation/gaps), this can create a steady CPU cost. This is a performance/scalability concern grounded in the diff, not a correctness bug per se.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Per-message metrics.gauge emission of queue_depth in the worker hot path adds real per-message overhead at high throughput and should be sampled/aggregated

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a per-work-item metrics emission in the hot path: in `OrderedQueueWorker.run()` the `finally` block calls `metrics.gauge("remote_subscriptions.queue_worker.queue_depth", self.work_queue.qsize(), ...)` for every processed message. At high throughput this can create measurable overhead (metric call + `qsize()` + tags) and increased metrics volume. This is a performance/operational concern rather than a correctness defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: sentry_sdk.start_transaction is called per work item, adding significant per-message overhead on high-volume topics; batching or sampling is advisable

adjudication.rationale: In `src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py`, `OrderedQueueWorker.run` wraps every dequeued `work_item` in `sentry_sdk.start_transaction(...)` before calling `self.result_processor(...)`. This is clearly per-message instrumentation and could add significant overhead on high-volume topics; it’s a performance/observability design concern rather than a correctness defect. The diff does not show any batching or sampling to mitigate that overhead.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Failed messages are committed as processed: complete_offset() is called unconditionally in the finally block even when result_processor raises, causing permanent data loss with no retry, dead-letter, or offset rollback

adjudication.rationale: In `OrderedQueueWorker.run`, `offset_tracker.complete_offset(work_item.partition, work_item.offset)` is executed in the `finally` block regardless of whether `self.result_processor(...)` succeeds or raises (the generic `except Exception` only logs). Since the commit loop in `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy._commit_loop` commits any contiguous offsets reported as completed, a failed processing attempt will still be treated as processed and eventually committed, with no retry/requeue/dead-letter handling shown in this diff—creating a clear risk of permanent message loss.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Shutdown race drops queued items: shutdown() sets worker.shutdown flag before q.shutdown, so worker exits after current item leaving remaining queued items unprocessed despite graceful shutdown semantics

adjudication.rationale: In `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` (new file `queue_consumer.py`), the code sets `worker.shutdown = True` for all workers before calling `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` on the queues. Each `OrderedQueueWorker.run()` loop is `while not self.shutdown:` and only calls `work_queue.get()` inside that loop. Once `shutdown` is set, after finishing its current item the worker will exit the loop and stop consuming, even if the queue still contains items. Since `queue.shutdown(immediate=False)` is intended to allow draining remaining items (raising `queue.ShutDown` only once empty), this ordering can leave queued items unprocessed, matching the finding’s “drops queued items” claim.

adjudication_records.issue_text: No backpressure: queue.Queue() is unbounded and submit() never blocks, allowing unbounded memory growth/OOM if consumers ingest faster than workers process

adjudication.rationale: In `FixedQueuePool.__init__`, each worker queue is created as `queue.Queue()` with no `maxsize`, so it is unbounded. In `FixedQueuePool.submit`, `work_queue.put(work_item)` will therefore never block due to capacity (it only blocks when `maxsize>0`). This contradicts the stated guarantee in `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` (“Natural backpressure when queues fill up”) and can allow unbounded memory growth/OOM if ingestion outpaces worker processing.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Worker thread death is silent and permanently stalls the partition: exceptions in the finally block (complete_offset, metrics.gauge) kill the worker thread with no watchdog or health signal, stalling all groups hashed to that queue

adjudication.rationale: In `OrderedQueueWorker.run`, the `finally` block calls `self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(...)` and `metrics.gauge(...)` without any guarding `try/except` (new file `queue_consumer.py`). If either of those calls were to raise, the exception would escape `run()` (it is not covered by the inner `except Exception:` which precedes the `finally`) and the worker thread would terminate, leaving its queue unserviced and offsets potentially permanently outstanding. The diff does not prove those calls can raise in practice, so this is a robustness/operability concern rather than a strictly verifiable defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: join() misuses arroyo's shutdown protocol: join() calls close(), ignoring the timeout parameter, so shutdown can take up to 5 + 5×num_queues seconds and may force-terminate mid-flight

adjudication.rationale: In `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.join(self, timeout: float | None = None)`, the `timeout` parameter is ignored and it unconditionally calls `self.close()`. `close()` then blocks with fixed timeouts: `self.commit_thread.join(timeout=5.0)` and `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` joins each worker with `worker.join(timeout=5.0)` in a loop, so shutdown latency can exceed any caller-provided `timeout` and scale with `num_queues`. The diff does not show any logic to honor `timeout` or to bound total wait time.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Final offsets never committed on graceful shutdown: close() sets shutdown_event before draining, so the commit loop exits without a final commit pass, causing full redelivery of drained work on restart

adjudication.rationale: In `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()`, `shutdown_event` is set and the `commit_thread` is joined **before** shutting down the `queue_pool`/workers. That means the commit loop can stop (exit its `while not shutdown_event.is_set()` loop) while worker threads are still processing and calling `offset_tracker.complete_offset(...)` in `OrderedQueueWorker.run()`’s `finally`. Any offsets completed after the commit thread has exited will never be committed, so successfully processed messages can be redelivered after restart. There is also no drain step (e.g., `wait_until_empty`) before stopping commits.

adjudication_records.issue_text: No health-check or stall detection for the pipeline: no detection for persistent commit_function failures (offsets accumulate forever), poison groups backing up, and no alerting hooks

adjudication.rationale: The new `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` runs a background `_commit_loop` that calls `commit_function(committable)` inside a broad `except Exception: logger.exception("Error in commit loop")` and then continues (no retry/backoff/alert metric). If `commit_function` persistently fails, `OffsetTracker.mark_committed` is never reached, so `OffsetTracker.all_offsets` is never pruned (it is only pruned in `mark_committed`), meaning processed offsets can accumulate in memory while the system keeps processing (`submit` keeps calling `add_offset`). The diff also only emits a metric on successful commits (`offsets_committed`) and queue depth gauges, with no explicit stall/poison-group detection or failure metric/hook. This is a concrete operational/health gap grounded in the added code, but not a strictly immediate correctness bug.

adjudication_records.issue_text: submit()'s error path can complete an offset it never added: if put() raises ShutDown after add_offset, the handler marks the dropped item complete, causing silent loss during shutdown

adjudication.rationale: In `FixedQueuePool.submit`, the offset is added to `OffsetTracker` *before* `work_queue.put(work_item)`. If `put()` raises `queue.ShutDown` (or any exception), that exception propagates to `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit`, whose `except Exception` handler calls `add_offset(...)` and then `complete_offset(...)`. This will mark the offset as completed even though the work item was never enqueued/processed, allowing `_commit_loop` to treat it as committable and potentially commit past an unprocessed/dropped message (silent loss). The finding’s phrasing “never added” is slightly off (it may already have been added), but the underlying dropped-item-then-completed/committed behavior is supported by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Integration tests mock the processor entirely, verifying plumbing but not the feature — no test verifies thread-queue-parallel produces the same application-level results as serial mode

adjudication.rationale: The newly added thread-queue-parallel tests mostly validate wiring (that `result_processor` is invoked and offsets are committed) while mocking out the actual processing logic. For example, multiple new tests patch `type(factory.result_processor).__call__` (e.g. `test_thread_queue_parallel`, `test_thread_queue_parallel_preserves_order`, `test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling`, and the Kafka integration test) so they don't assert any real application-level side effects/results compared to serial mode. The diff does add unit tests for ordering/offset tracking in `test_queue_consumer.py`, but it does not add a test demonstrating that the new mode produces the same domain outcomes as existing serial processing.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Error-handling test asserts no commit for failed partition, contradicting implementation which calls complete_offset even on exception, so failed messages are silently skipped; no reliable test pins down intended at-least-once vs skip-on-error semantics

adjudication.rationale: The implementation marks offsets complete even when processing fails: `OrderedQueueWorker.run` catches `Exception` from `self.result_processor(...)` but then *always* calls `self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(...)` in `finally`. The commit loop in `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy._commit_loop` will then treat that offset as processed and commit it once contiguous, effectively skipping/losing failed messages. This contradicts the strategy docstring (“Only commits offsets after successful processing”) and also conflicts with the new test `test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling`, which asserts no commit should occur for the partition after a processing exception.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Rebalance bug: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close shuts down the shared queue pool and workers, but ResultsStrategyFactory reuses the dead pool when creating a new strategy via create_with_partitions, causing silent data loss or hangs after rebalance; no close-then-recreate test exists

adjudication.rationale: In `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close` (new file `queue_consumer.py`), it calls `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`, which stops worker threads and calls `q.shutdown(...)` on each underlying `queue.Queue`. However, `ResultsStrategyFactory` stores a single `self.queue_pool` created in `__init__` for `mode == "thread-queue-parallel"` and then reuses it in `create_thread_queue_parallel_worker` / `create_with_partitions` without recreating or checking whether it was previously shut down. After a rebalance, the old strategy’s `close()` would shut down the shared pool, and a subsequent `create_with_partitions` would hand a new `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` the already-dead pool. Subsequent `FixedQueuePool.submit()` -> `work_queue.put()` would likely raise `queue.ShutDown`, which is caught in `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit` and then marks the offset complete, risking silent message loss. The diff’s tests don’t cover close-then-recreate/rebalance behavior.

adjudication_records.issue_text: join() calls close() and shuts down the queue pool, deviating from arroyo strategy lifecycle where join should only wait for in-flight work; no test covers close/join/terminate lifecycle ordering

adjudication.rationale: In `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` (new file `queue_consumer.py`), `join()` is implemented as `self.close()` (lines near end), and `close()` sets `shutdown_event`, joins the commit thread, and calls `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`. This means calling `join()` will actively shut down the strategy/worker pool rather than only waiting for in-flight work, which can deviate from the expected arroyo `ProcessingStrategy` lifecycle (where `close/terminate` initiate shutdown and `join` waits). The tests added exercise processing/ordering/commits, but none cover `close()` vs `join()` vs `terminate()` ordering/idempotency (e.g., calling `close()` then `join()`, or `terminate()` then `join()`).

adjudication_records.issue_text: test_stats_reporting asserts stats["total_items"] > 0 immediately after submitting, a timing-dependent race that makes the test flaky

adjudication.rationale: In `tests/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/test_queue_consumer.py::TestFixedQueuePool.test_stats_reporting`, the test submits 10 items and immediately does `stats = self.pool.get_stats(); assert stats["total_items"] > 0`. Since `FixedQueuePool` starts daemon worker threads in `__init__` and `submit()` enqueues work that can be processed immediately, it’s possible for the workers to drain all queues before the `get_stats()` call runs, making `total_items == 0` and causing a timing-dependent failure (flaky test).

adjudication_records.issue_text: No test that group→queue assignment ordering survives process restarts, given hash() is salt-randomized per process for strings in FixedQueuePool.get_queue_for_group

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `FixedQueuePool.get_queue_for_group` uses Python’s built-in `hash(group_key) % self.num_queues` for “consistent hashing”. For `str`, `hash()` is salt-randomized per process by default, so group→queue mapping will change across process restarts. The newly added tests only validate consistency within a single process run (e.g. `test_consistent_group_assignment`) and do not cover restart stability. This is a real, diff-grounded review concern about the intended “consistent” behavior, but it is not a clearly verifiable correctness defect in the diff by itself.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Factory test only asserts types, never submitting a message, so factory wiring (decoder, grouping function, +1 offset commit semantics) is unverified at the factory level

adjudication.rationale: While the `TestThreadQueueParallelIntegration.test_factory_creates_thread_queue_parallel_strategy` only asserts the strategy type and `num_queues` without submitting messages, the diff adds multiple factory-level tests in `tests/sentry/uptime/consumers/test_results_consumer.py` that do submit messages through `UptimeResultsStrategyFactory.create_with_partitions(...)` and verify decoding/processing and the factory’s `commit_offsets` +1 semantics (e.g. `test_thread_queue_parallel_offset_commit` expects committed offset 105 for processed 100–104, and `test_thread_queue_parallel_offset_gaps` expects commit 101 after processing 100). Therefore, the claim that factory wiring (+1 commit, decoder/grouping usage) is unverified at the factory level is not supported by the diff as a whole.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Processing errors are swallowed and the offset is still marked complete: complete_offset is called in finally in the worker's except Exception path, so failed messages (e.g., transient DB errors) are permanently committed and never retried, causing silent message loss

adjudication.rationale: In `OrderedQueueWorker.run`, any exception from `self.result_processor(...)` is caught and logged (`except Exception:`), but the `finally` block still calls `self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(work_item.partition, work_item.offset)`. Since `FixedQueuePool.submit` always calls `offset_tracker.add_offset(...)` before enqueuing, a failed work item will be marked complete anyway. The commit thread in `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy._commit_loop` uses `get_committable_offsets()` to decide what to commit, so once the failed offset is marked complete it can become committable and be committed, with no retry/requeue path shown in the diff. This can lead to permanent loss of messages on transient processing errors.

adjudication_records.issue_text: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy docstring claims 'Only commits offsets after successful processing' but the code commits offsets even on failure, violating the documented guarantee

adjudication.rationale: The docstring for `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` promises "Only commits offsets after successful processing", but in `OrderedQueueWorker.run` the offset is marked complete in a `finally:` block unconditionally, even when `result_processor(...)` raises (caught by `except Exception:`). Once `OffsetTracker.complete_offset(...)` is called, `_commit_loop` can treat that offset as processed and commit it via `commit_function`, meaning failed messages may still be committed (data-loss risk) and the docstring guarantee is violated.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Strategy close() destroys the shared FixedQueuePool by calling queue_pool.shutdown(), breaking rebalances/restarts since create_with_partitions reuses the now-dead pool and submitted messages sit forever in queues with no consumer

adjudication.rationale: In `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` the strategy unconditionally calls `self.queue_pool.shutdown()` (src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py), which stops the worker threads/queues. But in `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__`, the `FixedQueuePool` is created once and stored on the factory (`self.queue_pool = FixedQueuePool(...)`), and `create_with_partitions()` reuses that same `self.queue_pool` for each new strategy (`assert self.queue_pool is not None` then pass it into `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy`). The factory does not recreate the pool when a strategy is closed, and `close()` does not null out `factory.queue_pool`. Therefore, if the processor closes a strategy (e.g., during partition revoke/rebalance) and then calls `create_with_partitions()` again on the same factory instance, the new strategy will reuse a shutdown/dead pool, so submitted work may never be processed.

adjudication_records.issue_text: The 'natural backpressure' claim is false because queues are unbounded (queue.Queue() has no maxsize), so submit never blocks and memory grows unboundedly if processing is slower than consumption

adjudication.rationale: In `FixedQueuePool.__init__`, each worker queue is created as `queue.Queue()` with no `maxsize`, making it unbounded. `FixedQueuePool.submit` calls `work_queue.put(work_item)` with no timeout, so submission will not block as load increases. This contradicts the `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` docstring claim of “Natural backpressure when queues fill up” and can allow unbounded memory growth if consumption outpaces processing.

adjudication_records.issue_text: wait_until_empty / get_stats()['total_items'] == 0 is not a completion signal since qsize() == 0 only means items were dequeued and the worker may still be processing the last item, making tests that poll on this racy

adjudication.rationale: In `FixedQueuePool.get_stats()` / `wait_until_empty()`, `total_items` is computed from `q.qsize()` for each queue. In `OrderedQueueWorker.run()`, the queue size drops as soon as `work_queue.get()` dequeues the item, *before* `result_processor(...)` runs and before `offset_tracker.complete_offset(...)` is called (it happens in `finally`). Therefore `get_stats()["total_items"] == 0` (and `wait_until_empty` returning True) can occur while the last dequeued item is still being processed, so it is not a reliable “all work complete” signal. The added tests that poll `queue_pool.get_stats()["total_items"] == 0` (e.g. in `tests/sentry/uptime/consumers/test_results_consumer.py`) are thus potentially racy.

adjudication_records.issue_text: wait_until_empty is dead code, never called anywhere

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `FixedQueuePool.wait_until_empty` is newly added in `queue_consumer.py`, and there are no calls to it within this diff. However, the finding claims it is "never called anywhere," which cannot be verified from the PR diff alone (it could be used in unchanged files). At most, it’s “unused in this diff,” not provably dead code repo-wide.

adjudication_records.issue_text: WorkItem.message is dead weight: set everywhere (forcing tests to construct fake Message objects) but never read, and it leaks arroyo KafkaPayload/Message types across the boundary

adjudication.rationale: In `queue_consumer.py`, `WorkItem` includes `message: Message[KafkaPayload | FilteredPayload]`, and callers always populate it (e.g. `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit` creates `WorkItem(..., message=message)`, and tests construct full `Message(BrokerValue(...))`). However, the worker path only uses `work_item.result`, `work_item.partition`, and `work_item.offset` (`OrderedQueueWorker.run` calls `result_processor(..., work_item.result)` and then `complete_offset(work_item.partition, work_item.offset)`), and the commit logic uses only the tracker. So `WorkItem.message` is currently unused/dead weight and also unnecessarily couples this internal queue abstraction to Arroyo `Message`/Kafka payload types.

adjudication_records.issue_text: max_workers is semantically overloaded as 'number of queues' (hash shards) rather than thread count, so changing one meaning silently changes the other, and 'or 20' fallback means --max-workers 0 silently becomes 20

adjudication.rationale: In `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__`, the new `thread-queue-parallel` mode constructs `FixedQueuePool(..., num_queues=max_workers or 20)`. Because this uses Python truthiness, a CLI-provided `--max-workers 0` (valid `int` per `click.Option(type=int)`) will be treated as false and silently replaced with `20`, changing the user’s configured parallelism unexpectedly. This behavior is directly introduced by the diff and is likely incorrect/misleading given `--max-workers` is described as “maximum amount of parallelism”.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Dead/nonsensical except queue.ShutDown around the result processor callback, which cannot raise queue.ShutDown — leftover copy-paste obscuring the actual exception path

adjudication.rationale: In `OrderedQueueWorker.run` (new `queue_consumer.py`), there is an `except queue.ShutDown:` both around `work_queue.get()` (where it makes sense if `Queue.shutdown()` is used) and again around the `result_processor(...)` callback. The diff provides no path showing `result_processor` would raise `queue.ShutDown`, so this second handler appears to be leftover/defensive copy-paste and could silently swallow an unexpected `queue.ShutDown` from elsewhere, obscuring real errors. This is a concrete diff-grounded cleanliness/clarity issue but not a verifiable functional defect on its own.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Commit thread is started in __init__, making the object impossible to construct without side effects (tests must always call close/shutdown or leak threads)

adjudication.rationale: In `src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py`, `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.__init__` unconditionally starts a background thread (`self.commit_thread = threading.Thread(...); self.commit_thread.start()`), and `FixedQueuePool.__init__` starts worker threads immediately (`worker.start()` in the constructor). This makes constructing these objects have side effects (spawning threads) and requires callers/tests to always call `close()`/`shutdown()` to avoid leaking threads, matching the finding. The diff does include `close()/shutdown()` paths, but the side-effectful construction concern is still valid and diff-grounded.

adjudication_records.issue_text: join() delegates to close(), conflating arroyo's join (wait for completion) with close (stop), so graceful draining isn't implemented and in-flight items are dropped when close runs

adjudication.rationale: In `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy`, `join()` unconditionally calls `self.close()` (new file `queue_consumer.py`, `def join(...): self.close()`). `close()` sets `shutdown_event` and then calls `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`, which sets `worker.shutdown = True` for all workers before shutting down the queues. Each `OrderedQueueWorker.run()` loop is `while not self.shutdown: ... get() ... process ...`, so setting `shutdown=True` causes the worker to stop even if `work_queue` still contains items, i.e. it does not drain. Therefore `join()` (which should wait for completion/drain) instead initiates shutdown and can drop queued/in-flight work, matching the finding.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Shared FixedQueuePool is destroyed when any strategy closes/rebalances, shutting down all worker threads and queues for other still-live strategies, silently dropping messages on routine rebalances

adjudication.rationale: In `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__`, `self.queue_pool` is created once and stored on the factory when `mode == "thread-queue-parallel"` (so it is shared across any `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` instances produced by `create_with_partitions`). However, `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` (and `terminate()`) unconditionally calls `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`. That means when Arroyo closes a strategy (e.g., on partition revocation/rebalance), it will shut down the shared `FixedQueuePool` worker threads/queues, and subsequent strategies created by the same factory will reuse an already-shutdown pool. This matches the finding’s core claim that a shared pool can be destroyed by a single strategy’s lifecycle, breaking processing after routine rebalances.

adjudication_records.issue_text: join() calls close(), causing the shared pool to be shut down twice on normal graceful shutdown

adjudication.rationale: In `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy`, `join()` unconditionally calls `self.close()` (see `def join(...): self.close()`). `close()` shuts down the commit thread and calls `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`. If the surrounding Arroyo lifecycle calls `close()` and then `join()` (a common pattern), this will attempt to shut down the same shared `FixedQueuePool` a second time, potentially triggering exceptions/log noise (e.g., repeated `q.shutdown(...)` / worker joins) and violating expected `join()` semantics (wait-only).

adjudication_records.issue_text: OrderedQueueWorker.run completes the offset in the finally block even when result_processor raised, causing failed messages to be committed as processed (permanent silent data loss)

adjudication.rationale: In `OrderedQueueWorker.run`, `offset_tracker.complete_offset(...)` is executed in the `finally` block even when `result_processor(...)` raises (caught by the broad `except Exception`). That marks failed messages as completed, allowing `OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets()` in the commit loop to advance and `commit_function` to commit those offsets as processed, dropping the failed message with no retry path. This contradicts the strategy docstring claim “Only commits offsets after successful processing.”

adjudication_records.issue_text: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit's catch-all marks decode/grouping_fn failures as complete, committing offsets for failed messages

adjudication.rationale: In `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit`, the `except Exception:` handler unconditionally calls `offset_tracker.add_offset(...)` and `complete_offset(...)` for the message’s partition/offset. This marks the message as successfully processed even when failures come from `decoder(...)`, `grouping_fn(...)`, or other submit-time errors, allowing the commit loop to eventually commit past that offset and effectively drop the failed message (contradicting the class docstring claim of committing only after successful processing).

adjudication_records.issue_text: Test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling passes only by timing luck with an or-escape-hatch assertion, masking the data-loss bug (silent-pass verification mechanism)

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces a real data-loss risk: `OrderedQueueWorker.run()` calls `self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(...)` in a `finally:` block even when `result_processor(...)` raises (it only logs the exception). This makes failed messages appear “processed” and therefore committable in `OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets()`, so the commit loop can advance offsets past failed work. The cited test `test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling` also appears timing-dependent and weakly asserted (`assert len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`), so it can pass without reliably detecting the bad commit behavior, aligning with the finding’s claim that it can mask the bug.

adjudication_records.issue_text: If FixedQueuePool.shutdown races with a put, queue.Queue.put raises ShutDown in submit(), and the catch-all marks that offset complete, losing the message

adjudication.rationale: In `FixedQueuePool.submit`, the offset is recorded (`offset_tracker.add_offset(...)`) before `work_queue.put(work_item)`. During `FixedQueuePool.shutdown`, each queue is shut down via `q.shutdown(immediate=False)`, which can cause subsequent `Queue.put(...)` calls to raise `queue.ShutDown`. That exception propagates up to `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit`, which wraps the whole submit path in `except Exception:` and, on error, calls `add_offset`/`complete_offset` for that message’s partition/offset. Net effect: if shutdown races with `put`, the message is never enqueued/processed, but its offset is marked complete and becomes committable (data loss). This behavior is directly implied by the new code in `queue_consumer.py` (`FixedQueuePool.submit`, `FixedQueuePool.shutdown`, and `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit`).

adjudication_records.issue_text: Queues are unbounded (queue.Queue() with no maxsize), providing no backpressure despite the design claim, risking OOM under load

adjudication.rationale: In `FixedQueuePool.__init__`, each work queue is created as `queue.Queue()` with no `maxsize` (default `maxsize=0`, i.e. unbounded). In `submit`, items are added via `work_queue.put(work_item)` with no bounding or blocking behavior. This contradicts the stated guarantee in `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` (“Natural backpressure when queues fill up”) and can allow unbounded memory growth/OOM under load since the producer side will not be backpressured by queue capacity.

adjudication_records.issue_text: terminate() never joins the commit thread and never commits final offsets, losing up to the last second of processed offsets and racing with pool teardown

adjudication.rationale: In `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy`, `close()` sets `shutdown_event`, joins `commit_thread`, and then shuts down the queue pool. But `terminate()` only sets `shutdown_event` and immediately calls `self.queue_pool.shutdown()` without joining `commit_thread` or draining/committing remaining committable offsets. The commit loop runs on a 1s cadence (`shutdown_event.wait(1.0)`), so `terminate()` can exit before the next commit cycle and can also race with pool teardown since `commit_thread` may still execute while `queue_pool.shutdown()` is in progress.

adjudication_records.issue_text: OffsetTracker's mark_committed never prunes outstanding offsets, so stale state after partition revoke/reassign can permanently block commits for that partition, stalling the consumer

adjudication.rationale: In `OffsetTracker.mark_committed`, the code prunes `all_offsets[partition]` for offsets `<= committed`, but does not touch `outstanding`. While that is technically true, the commitability logic in `get_committable_offsets` only considers offsets that are present in `all_offsets` (it checks `if offset in all_offsets and offset not in outstanding`). Since `mark_committed` removes committed offsets from `all_offsets`, any stale `outstanding` entries for those offsets will not block future commits. The diff also shows no partition revoke/reassign handling, so the claim about stale state after revoke permanently blocking commits cannot be verified from this PR diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: There is no rebalance hook to reset or hand off OffsetTracker state

adjudication.rationale: The new thread-queue-parallel path introduces long-lived per-partition offset state in `OffsetTracker` (stored on `FixedQueuePool`, created in `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__`) and a background commit loop (`SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy._commit_loop`) that will continue to compute/commit offsets for whatever partitions remain in the tracker. The diff shows no mechanism to clear per-partition state on partition revocation / rebalance (no hook/API to drop a partition from `OffsetTracker`, and no rebalance callback wiring in this new strategy), so on reassignments the tracker could retain offsets for partitions no longer owned. This is a rebalance/architecture gap grounded in the added classes, even if the exact rebalance lifecycle isn’t shown in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: submit() catch-all converts every decoder/grouping_fn bug into silent message loss with only a log line, degrading ordering guarantees silently

adjudication.rationale: In `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit`, the broad `except Exception` logs and then immediately calls `add_offset` + `complete_offset` for the message’s partition/offset (when `message.value` is a `BrokerValue`). That marks the message as successfully processed even if the failure happened in `decoder(...)`, `grouping_fn(...)`, or queue submission, allowing the commit loop to advance offsets and permanently skip the failed message. This contradicts the stated guarantees ("Only commits offsets after successful processing") and results in real message loss (not a retry or dead-letter path).

adjudication_records.issue_text: hash(group_key) is process-randomized (PYTHONHASHSEED), breaking cross-process consistency and the docstring's consistent-hashing claim; should use a stable hash like md5

adjudication.rationale: In `FixedQueuePool.get_queue_for_group` the code uses `hash(group_key) % self.num_queues`, and the pool is explicitly a per-process, in-memory threading construct (one worker thread per queue). The ordering/assignment guarantee described in the docstring (“consistently assigned to the same queue”) is satisfied within a single process lifetime even with Python’s hash randomization; nothing in the diff claims or requires cross-process/run stability. Therefore the finding’s “breaking cross-process consistency” and “docstring’s consistent-hashing claim” assertions are not a verifiable defect from this diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Test test_different_groups_distributed asserts an exact probabilistic distribution (all 3 queues hit), which is flaky

adjudication.rationale: In `tests/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/test_queue_consumer.py::TestFixedQueuePool.test_different_groups_distributed`, the test collects `hash(group_key) % 3` for 20 group keys and asserts `len(queue_indices) == 3`. Since Python’s `hash()` is salted per process and not guaranteed to cover all residues modulo 3 for a fixed set of inputs, it’s possible (though low probability) that only 1–2 queues are hit, making this assertion flaky. This is a test robustness issue, not a production correctness defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: wait_until_empty checks qsize()==0 which does not mean items are processed (in-flight items), making it misleading/unsafe if used for shutdown

adjudication.rationale: In `FixedQueuePool.wait_until_empty`, emptiness is determined via `self.get_stats()["total_items"] == 0`, and `get_stats` uses `q.qsize()` (diff: `queue_depths = [q.qsize() for q in self.queues]`). A worker can `get()` an item (making `qsize()` drop to 0) while still processing it, so `wait_until_empty` can return `True` even though work is still in-flight. The method’s docstring only promises “queues are empty” (not “all items processed”), and it is not used for shutdown in this diff, so this is a misleading/unsafe helper rather than a demonstrated functional defect.
